problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=6{x}^{2}-{x}^{4}$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x)$ is concave up on $(-1,1)$
- $f(x)$ is concave up on $(-\infty ,-1)$
- $f(x)$ is concave down on $(0,\infty )$
worked_solution:
First, we calculate the second derivative of $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =12x-4{x}^{3} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =12-12{x}^{2} \\  & =12(1-{x}^{2}) \\  & =12(1+x)(1-x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the function is concave up, we need to solve ${f}^{″}(x)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12(1+x)(1-x) & >0 \\ (x+1)(x-1) & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this inequality by considering the graph of $y=(x+1)(x-1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067662/assets/09b4b237ec87a63e6de47eea5ed9156febbed0271dd0688c0be1c22a62c50c4e.png)

From the graph, we see that $(x+1)(x-1)<0$ when $-1<x<1.$ So the graph is concave up on the interval $(-1,1).$

The function $f(x)$ is concave down when ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ By similar reasoning to before, this leads to the inequality $(x+1)(x-1)>0,$ which has the solutions $(-\infty ,-1)$ and $(1,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
